\chapter{Primeiro, Segundo, Terceiro}
\label{ch:pt-ordinais}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Portuguese with the right gender, and say why the week starts at the second day and why Tuesday is terca and not terceira.}

The fifth ordinal said against the four before it, with the weekday it names and the farm that was named for the fifth of its harvest.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[primeiro / primeira]{primeiro — first, and the day the week left out}

\label{lesson:PT-C27-primeiro}



\begin{quote}
A new kind of counting starts here, so the recalls come first, at the four growing distances this book measures.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a boca e o coração} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o café} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o pão} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a água e o vinho} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{olá} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bom / boa} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{primeiro} (masculine) · \textbf{primeira} (feminine) — \textbf{first}. \textbf{o primeiro dia} — the first day. \textbf{a primeira vez} — the first time.
\end{quote}

\emph{Um, dois, três} answer \textbf{how many}. This word answers \textbf{which one in the line}, and Portuguese keeps a second series of words for that job. Like any describing word it changes its ending with what it counts.

\begin{culture}
The weekday chapter left a question open on purpose: why does \emph{segunda-feira} mean \textquotedblleft{}second feast-day\textquotedblright{} when it is the \textbf{first} day of the working week?

Because it is not the first day of the \textbf{week}. \textbf{Domingo} is — \emph{diēs Dominica}, \textquotedblleft{}the Lord's day\textquotedblright{} — and it was counted as the first. So the numbering starts at \emph{domingo}, Monday lands on \textbf{two}, and Portuguese never needed a \emph{primeira-feira}. The one ordinal that is missing from the week is the one that explains it.

\emph{Primeiro} itself comes not from Latin \emph{prīmus} but from \emph{\textbf{prīmārius}}, \textquotedblleft{}of the first rank\textquotedblright{} — the same shape behind English \textbf{primary} and \textbf{premier}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{primeiro, primeira}
  \item \emph{o primeiro dia} — the first day
  \item \emph{domingo é o primeiro dia} — and that is why Monday is \emph{segunda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the first time.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{A primeira vez}.) Why is Monday \emph{segunda-feira} and not the first? (\textbf{Domingo is counted first}, so the numbering starts there.) And which Latin word is \emph{primeiro} built on? (\emph{\textbf{Prīmārius}}, \textquotedblleft{}of the first rank\textquotedblright{} — not \emph{prīmus}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[segundo / segunda]{segundo — the word already in your week}

\label{lesson:PT-C27-segundo}



\begin{quote}
Recalls before the second ordinal, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{primeiro} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o chá} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o olho} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{onze a quinze} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dezasseis a vinte} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o / a} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dia} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{segundo} (masculine) · \textbf{segunda} (feminine) — \textbf{second}. \textbf{o segundo andar} — the second floor. \textbf{a segunda vez} — the second time.
\end{quote}

You have been saying the feminine every week without knowing it was a number word: \emph{\textbf{segunda\emph{-feira\textbf{ is exactly this, with \emph{feira} attached.}}}}

\begin{cousinweb}
There is no \emph{dois} in \emph{segundo}, and there was never meant to be. It comes from Latin \emph{\textbf{sequī}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to follow}\textquotedblright{} — so second place is named for what it does, the place that \textbf{comes after}, rather than for the count it sits at.

English borrowed the whole family: \textbf{second} is this word; so are \textbf{sequel}, \textbf{sequence}, \textbf{consequence} and \textbf{subsequent}, and every one still has \textquotedblleft{}follow\textquotedblright{} inside it.

And the \emph{segundo} on a clock is the same word. The Romans cut the hour into a \emph{pars minūta prīma}, \textquotedblleft{}the first small part\textquotedblright{} — our \textbf{minute} — and cut that again into a \emph{pars minūta secunda}. Portuguese kept the adjective and dropped the noun, so \textbf{um segundo} is literally \textquotedblleft{}a following one\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{segundo, segunda}
  \item \emph{segunda-feira} — the second feast-day
  \item \emph{um segundo} — a second, the second cutting of the hour
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{segundo} built on? (\emph{\textbf{Sequī}}, to follow.) So what is second place, in Portuguese's own terms? (\textbf{The place that comes after}.) And what is \emph{um segundo} on a clock, taken apart? (\textbf{The second small part} of the hour, after the \textbf{minute}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[terceiro / terceira]{terceiro — one Latin word, two Portuguese children}

\label{lesson:PT-C27-terceiro}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the third ordinal — the one that does not match its weekday.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{segundo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o leite} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a orelha} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{preto e branco} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vermelho e azul} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bom dia} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{boa tarde} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{terceiro} (masculine) · \textbf{terceira} (feminine) — \textbf{third}. \textbf{o terceiro dia} — the third day. \textbf{a terceira vez} — the third time.
\end{quote}

Now look at Tuesday. It is \emph{\textbf{terça\emph{-feira\textbf{, not \emph{terceira-feira}.}}}}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two children of one word}]
Latin \emph{tertius} left \textbf{two} descendants in Portuguese, and both survive:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{where it lives} \\
\midrule
\textbf{terça} & frozen in \emph{terça-feira}, and in \textbf{um terço}, \textquotedblleft{}a third part\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{terceiro} & the ordinary counting word — \emph{o terceiro andar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Terça} is the older, inherited shape, worn down in ordinary speech; \emph{terceiro} was rebuilt later on the pattern of \emph{primeiro}. The week was numbered in the sixth century and kept the shape that existed then, which is why Tuesday looks older than the word for \textquotedblleft{}third\textquotedblright{} — it is.

So \emph{quarta} and \emph{quinta} will match their ordinals exactly, and this one does not. Watch for it: it is the only weekday that disagrees.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{terceiro, terceira}
  \item the two children — \emph{terça-feira} and \emph{o terceiro andar}
  \item \emph{um terço} — a third part
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which weekday is Tuesday, and why is it not \emph{terceira-feira}? (\emph{\textbf{Terça\emph{-feira\textbf{ — it kept the older, inherited shape.) What does \emph{um terço} mean? (}A third part\textbf{.) And which of the two forms would you use to say \textquotedblleft{}the third floor\textquotedblright{}? (}}O terceiro andar}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quarto / quarta]{quarto — the ordinal that is also Wednesday, and also a bedroom}

\label{lesson:PT-C27-quarto}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the fourth — and the shape that carries the rest of the way.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{terceiro} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o queijo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{a boca} — \textbf{R2}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ter} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{falei} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{boa noite} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{obrigado / obrigada} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quarto} (masculine) · \textbf{quarta} (feminine) — \textbf{fourth}. \textbf{o quarto andar} — the fourth floor. \textbf{a quarta vez} — the fourth time.
\end{quote}

And Wednesday is \emph{\textbf{quarta\emph{-feira\textbf{ — the feminine of this word, unchanged. After \emph{terça}'s split, the series settles: the number you already know, wearing an ending, agreeing with what it counts.}}}}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Quatro} is four; \emph{quarto} is four with the ordinal ending, and you can hear the cardinal inside it.

\textbf{O quarto} also means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a bedroom}\textquotedblright{}, and that is the same word doing a second job: a \emph{quarta parte}, a \textbf{fourth part} of a house, became the name for a room in it. English keeps exactly this in \textbf{quarters} — \textquotedblleft{}the servants' quarters\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}close quarters\textquotedblright{} — and in a \textbf{quart}, a fourth of a gallon.

So one Portuguese word covers \textquotedblleft{}fourth\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}Wednesday\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}bedroom\textquotedblright{}, and all three are the same idea seen from different rooms.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quarto, quarta}
  \item \emph{quarta-feira} — Wednesday, the fourth feast-day
  \item \emph{o meu quarto} — my bedroom, a fourth part of the house
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the fourth floor.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{O quarto andar}.) What is \emph{quarta-feira}, taken literally? (\textbf{The fourth feast-day} — Wednesday.) And why does \emph{o quarto} mean a bedroom? (\textbf{A fourth part} of a house — English \emph{quarters} does the same.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quinto / quinta]{quinto — the fifth, and the fifth of the harvest}

\label{lesson:PT-C27-quinto}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the fifth — and a word you will see on every wine label.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quarto} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{o ovo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ser} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sou, era, fui} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{de nada} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{como} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quinto} (masculine) · \textbf{quinta} (feminine) — \textbf{fifth}. \textbf{o quinto andar} — the fifth floor. \textbf{a quinta vez} — the fifth time.
\end{quote}

Thursday is \emph{\textbf{quinta\emph{-feira\textbf{, the feminine again unchanged. Note the vowel: \emph{cinco} is five, but the ordinal keeps the older \emph{qu-} of Latin \emph{quīntus}, so the two do not rhyme.}}}}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{A quinta} is a country estate or farm, and it is on the label of half the port in Portugal — \emph{Quinta do Noval}, \emph{Quinta da Boeira}. It is this ordinal.

A tenant once paid the landowner a share of what the land produced, and in Portugal that share was the \emph{\textbf{quinta parte}}, the \textbf{fifth part}. The land was named for its rent, the rent stopped being a fifth centuries ago, and the name stayed. So a Portuguese farm is a number, and the number is five.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quinto, quinta}
  \item \emph{quinta-feira} — Thursday, the fifth feast-day
  \item \emph{a quinta} — the farm named for its fifth
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the fifth time.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{A quinta vez}.) What is a \emph{quinta}, and where does the name come from? (\textbf{A farm} — from the \emph{quinta parte}, the \textbf{fifth} of the crop paid as rent.) And which day is \emph{quinta-feira}? (\textbf{Thursday}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
